title: Methodus nova et facilis calculum variationum tractandi

deep.reconstruction:
Setting: E420 treats a one-parameter family of curves. The ordinate y is a function of the abscissa x and a family parameter t. The principal curve is AM and the neighbouring curve is αμ, generated as the endpoint slides along a 'generating curve' BN. Euler writes partial derivatives in parentheses, e.g. (dy/dt) and (ddy/dx dt).

The variation of ∫Z dx splits into four parts:
- Part 1: the Euler–Lagrange integral term.
- Part 2: the boundary term carrying δy, multiplied by (P − dQ/dx + …).
- Part 3: the boundary term carrying δp, multiplied by (Q − dR/dx + …).
- Part 4: the boundary term carrying δq, and so on.

§43, finished at the top of this page, asks which Z make the boundary variation vanish when the endpoint is moved perpendicular to the curve. Put δy = −δx/p in Z δx + P(δy − p δx). This gives pZ = (1+p²)P. With x and y held fixed, P = ∂Z/∂p, so dZ/Z = p dp/(1+p²) and Z = V(x,y)√(1+p²). The functional is therefore ∫V ds. This page interprets it physically: if the speed at each point is 1/V for an arbitrary function V(x,y), then V dx√(1+p²) is the element of time and the integral is the travel time from A to M. This is a Fermat / brachistochrone-type travel-time functional.

§44 treats the third part, dt(ddy/dxdt)·(Q − dR/dx + d²S/dx² …). It is present only if Z contains second differentials. Mμ = dt(dy/dt) is the vertical displacement at M. At the next abscissa it is mω = Mμ + dt dx(ddy/dxdt). Hence dt(ddy/dxdt) = (mω − Mμ)/dx, which is δp. Euler reads this as the (infinitesimal) inclination of the varied tangent μω to the original tangent Mm.

§45 concludes: if the tangent at μ is parallel to the tangent at M, the third part vanishes. This happens when the generating curve BN has, at N, a tangent parallel to that of the main curve, and likewise at the initial end A/B. The next page adds that the fourth part also vanishes when the osculating radii agree.
errors: The last fraction is printed as (Mω − Mμ)/Pp. Consistency with the preceding (mω − Mμ)/dx requires mω in the numerator; Pp is the abscissa element dx. This is a printing slip (or a labelling inconsistency).
Calling δp the 'declinatio' (angle) is loose. The angle between the tangents is δp/(1+p²), not δp. This is harmless for Euler's purpose, since both vanish together.

Minor gap: the integration in §43 treats V as an arbitrary function of x and y, which is correct. Euler does not discuss the degenerate case p = 0 (or a vertical tangent) in the orthogonality condition.

ideas.what: Characterisation: the boundary variation vanishes under endpoint displacement normal to the curve iff Z = V(x,y)√(1+p²), interpreted as travel time with speed 1/V.
ideas.modern_name: Transversality coincides with orthogonality exactly for integrands F = f(x,y)√(1+y'²), i.e. Riemannian/Fermat-type functionals (Gauss-lemma-type property)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Transversality in general: Kneser (c.1900). Orthogonality for brachistochrones to a curve: the Bernoullis and Lagrange. The 'iff' appears as a standard textbook exercise (e.g. Gelfand–Fomin type).
ideas.where_published: E420 itself (Novi Comm. Acad. Petrop. 16, 1772), §43; Opera omnia I.25. Unsure whether Carathéodory's introduction highlights it.

ideas.what: Identification of the mixed partial variation dt(∂²y/∂x∂t) with the change of tangent direction, and the condition that the third (and fourth) boundary terms vanish if the comparison curves share tangents (and curvature) at the endpoints.
ideas.modern_name: Boundary terms for higher-order Lagrangians; fixed endpoint data (y, y', y'') kill the δy', δy'' terms
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler/Lagrange; standard in higher-order Euler–Poisson theory
ideas.where_published: E420 §§44–46; cf. the related E385 'Elementa calculi variationum'

missed.claim: Euler derives (at least in sufficiency/necessity form within his ansatz Q=R=0) that the only integrands whose free-endpoint variation vanishes for normal endpoint displacement are V(x,y)√(1+p²), with a kinematic (travel-time) interpretation. This is the converse statement of 'transversality = orthogonality', usually presented anonymously as a textbook exercise or attributed to the later Kneser theory of transversals.
missed.quote: Si enim celeritas in puncto M fuerit = 1/V ... tum V dx√(1+pp) exprimit elementum temporis
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Mainly historiographical: an early (1772) precursor of the transversality/orthogonality correspondence in Fermat-metric optics, worth crediting in histories of field theory. It is not mathematically new.

deep.surprise_reason: The page mostly finishes a known computation and explains routine boundary terms. The characterisation of Fermat-type integrands via orthogonal transversality is a nice early instance, but it is easy and likely noted by the Opera omnia editors.
transcription_corrections: The printed last fraction is (Mω − Mμ)/Pp. The transcription matches the print, but it should read (mω − Mμ)/Pp, consistent with the preceding (mω − Mμ)/dx.
'Explicatio partis tertiae in variatione' is a margin note in the print (Explicatio partis tertiae in va-riatione).
